title: Changing Face of the Earth: Landforms and Processes of Gradation
tagline: The landforms built by internal forces and the gradational work of running water, wind, glaciers and the sea.

overview.intro: Relief is always being built and always being worn down. Internal forces lift rock into mountains and plateaus, and gradational forces, driven by gravity and solar energy, cut, carry and deposit that material until relief is reduced toward a base level. This unit examines the major landforms produced by each process: the erosional and depositional work of rivers from youthful gorges to deltas, the work of wind in arid regions, the sculpting of glacial landscapes, and the coastlines shaped by the sea, together with the processes of weathering, erosion and deposition that underlie them all.

facts.label: Gradation
facts.value: The collective wearing down of relief by weathering, erosion and deposition, tending toward a base level.

facts.label: River stages
facts.value: Youthful: V-shaped valleys and gorges; mature: floodplains and meanders; old: broad valley, delta and braided channels.

facts.label: Base level
facts.value: The lowest level to which erosion can cut, taken as sea level for most purposes.

facts.label: Agents
facts.value: Running water, wind, glaciers and the sea, each with a characteristic set of landforms.

learningOutcomes: Describe the landforms created by a river in its youthful, mature and old stages.
Explain the work of wind and glaciers in forming landforms.
Explain the formation of a coastline feature and a delta.

blocks.text: Gradation is the general process by which relief is lowered, and it operates through four linked stages. Weathering breaks rock in place, either physically by frost, heat and root pressure, or chemically by solution, oxidation and carbonation. Erosion detaches and removes the weathered material, and it always requires an agent of transport. Transportation carries the load by water, wind, ice or gravity, and the capacity of the agent determines what size of particle can be moved. Deposition occurs when the agent loses energy, laying the material down and building new forms such as floodplains, dunes and deltas.

blocks.caption: The stages of gradation
rows: Rock broken in place by physical or chemical action
Detachment and removal of material by an agent
Movement of load by water, wind, ice or gravity
Material laid down as the agent loses energy

items: Weathering prepares material; erosion, transport and removal do the moving.
Kinetic energy of the agent depends on velocity, so faster flow carries coarser load.
The load of a river is dissolved, suspended or rolled along the bed.
Base level limits downward erosion, which is why valleys cannot deepen past it.
A graded stream is one in balance, eroding neither its bed nor its banks appreciably.

blocks.text: A river’s work changes with its gradient and stage. In the youthful stage the gradient is steep, downward erosion dominates and the valley is narrow and V-shaped, with interlocking spurs, waterfalls where a resistant rock band crosses the channel, and gorges cut into hard rock. In the mature stage the gradient eases, lateral erosion widens the valley floor, and meanders develop as the river swings against its banks, with slip-off slopes on the inside and cut banks outside.

In the old stage the river flows near base level, the valley is a broad floodplain, and the meanders migrate leaving ox-bow lakes when a neck of land is cut through. The load is finer and the river deposits it as natural levees during floods and as a broad delta where it enters a still sea. A delta builds outward because sediment supply exceeds the sea’s ability to remove it, and its distributary channels split across the deposit.

Meander, wider valley floor, slip-off slope and cut bank
Floodplain, natural levee, ox-bow lake, delta

blocks.text: In arid regions, where vegetation is sparse and material is loose, wind becomes a major agent. It erodes by deflation, removing fine particles and lowering a surface into a deflation hollow, and by abrasion as sand grains blast exposed rock, carving ventifacts and mushroom rocks with undercut bases. Wind also deposits material, building dunes whose shape records the wind, and laying down sheets of silt called loess, which can be tens of metres thick and is unusually fertile.

Glaciers erode by plucking, where meltwater freezes into rock and tears fragments away, and by abrasion as embedded rock grinds the bed like sandpaper. A glacial valley is typically U-shaped with a steep head and a truncating glacier, and the erosion produces cirques, arêtes and horns where several valleys eat into a ridge. When the ice melts, the transported material is deposited as till, forming moraines, drumlins and erratic boulders, while meltwater builds outwash plains and terraces.

learn.title: Work of the sea and coastal landforms

blocks.text: The sea attacks the land by hydraulic action, which forces air and water into cracks, by abrasion as wave-borne rock grinds the cliff, and by solution which dissolves soluble rock. The result is an erosional coast of cliffs, wave-cut platforms, arches, caves and stacks. Where the sea deposits material it builds beaches, spits, bars and tombolos, and a lagoon forms when a bar closes off an arm of the sea. The profile of a coast tends over long time to be smoothed toward a wave-cut abrasion platform at sea level.

items: Cliffs retreat as the notch at their base is undercut and the face collapses.
A wave-cut platform remains at the foot of a retreating cliff at low tide.
An arch collapses to leave a stack, which is eventually worn to a stump.
A spit grows from a headland when the longshore drift deposits material.
A bay head beach forms where waves refract around an indentation.

items.text: A sandbar closing a bay mouth and isolating brackish water.
items.note: A lagoon, which may become a lake as sediment and vegetation continue to fill it.

items.text: A mushroom rock with a narrow undercut base in a desert.
items.note: Abrasion concentrated near the ground where sand-laden wind travels fastest.

keyPoints: Gradation is the collective lowering of relief through weathering, erosion, transport and deposition.
Base level is the lowest level to which erosion can cut.
Youthful rivers erode downward, producing V-shaped valleys, gorges and waterfalls.
Mature rivers erode laterally, producing meanders with slip-off slopes and cut banks.
Old rivers deposit, producing floodplains, levees and deltas.
An ox-bow lake forms when a meander neck is cut through.
Wind erodes by deflation and abrasion and deposits dunes and loess.
Glaciers erode by plucking and abrasion, producing U-shaped valleys and cirques.
Glacial deposition leaves unsorted till as moraines and drumlins.
Wave erosion produces cliffs, arches, stacks and wave-cut platforms; wave deposition produces spits and bars.
examFocus: Landform answers should name the process first and the resulting form second, since attribution carries marks.
Diagrams earn marks when labelled, so practise a cross-section of a meander and a glacial trough.
Distinguish erosional from depositional features explicitly before describing each one.

questions.prompt: The V-shaped valley with steep sides is characteristic of which stage of a river?
questions.explanation: On a steep youthful gradient downward erosion dominates, so the valley is cut narrowly and deep rather than widened.

questions.prompt: An ox-bow lake is formed by:
options: A river cutting through a meander neck
questions.answer: A river cutting through a meander neck
questions.explanation: The river shortens its course across the narrow neck of a meander, isolating the abandoned bend as a crescent lake.

questions.prompt: U-shaped valleys, cirques and horns are characteristic landforms of:
questions.explanation: Glaciers widen and deepen a valley by plucking and abrasion, leaving a U-shaped trough, and competing glaciers sharpen ridges into arêtes and horns.

options: A thick deposit of wind-blown silt
questions.answer: A thick deposit of wind-blown silt
questions.explanation: Loess is fine silt carried by wind and deposited in sheets, and its fertility makes it valuable for farming.

questions.prompt: The lowest level to which erosion can cut is called the base __________ .
questions.explanation: Taken as sea level for most purposes, base level limits how deeply a river can deepen its valley.

questions.prompt: The process by which a glacier freezes rock to its base and tears fragments away is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Plucking works together with abrasion, which grinds the bed, to give a glacier its characteristic erosive power.

questions.prompt: State four landforms produced by a youthful river.
questions.answer: Four landforms are the V-shaped valley produced by downward erosion, the narrow gorge cut into resistant rock, the interlocking spur where the river winds between projecting ridges, and the waterfall formed where a resistant rock band crosses the channel and the softer rock below is cut back. A rapids reach is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each landform needs a line on the process that produced it, not merely the name.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the erosional and the depositional work of wind.
questions.answer: Wind erosion acts by deflation, which removes fine particles and lowers a surface into a deflation hollow, and by abrasion, where sand grains blast exposed rock to give ventifacts and mushroom rocks with undercut bases. Deposition occurs where wind loses velocity, building dunes whose shape reflects the wind direction and laying down sheets of fine silt known as loess, which can reach tens of metres in thickness. The material in wind deposits is well sorted by size, whereas glacial deposits are unsorted.
questions.explanation: Both halves are required with the landforms each produces and the energy condition that separates them.

questions.prompt: Describe the work of a river in its youthful, mature and old stages, giving the landforms of each.
questions.answer: In the youthful stage the gradient is steep and energy is directed downward, so the valley is narrow and V-shaped, with interlocking spurs where the channel bends around resistant rock, gorges cut in hard rock, and waterfalls where a resistant band crosses the stream. In the mature stage the gradient eases and lateral erosion becomes dominant, widening the valley floor; the river swings in meanders with a slip-off slope on the inside of the bend and a cut bank outside, and the banks are undercut until the outer curve collapses. In the old stage the river approaches base level, lateral swinging continues across a broad floodplain, and floods leave natural levees along the channel. Where a meander neck is cut through, the abandoned bend becomes an ox-bow lake. Finally, where the river enters a still sea it deposits its load and builds a delta with distributary channels, because sediment supply then exceeds the sea’s ability to remove it.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all three stages with the dominant process and at least two landforms named for each.

questions.prompt: A region shows rounded hilltops, thin unsorted deposits of mixed boulder and clay, and U-shaped valleys joining a main trough. Identify the agent responsible and account for each feature, then describe one form it leaves when it retreats.
questions.answer: The agent is a glacier. Rounded hilltops are the result of overriding ice stripping soil and smoothing bedrock as it passed. The unsorted deposit of boulders mixed with clay is glacial till, carried within and beneath the ice and dropped without sorting when the ice melted, which distinguishes it from river or wind deposits that separate material by size. The U-shaped valleys are glacial troughs, widened and deepened by plucking and abrasion until the former V-shaped river valley was reshaped, and their junction with the main trough shows tributary glaciers feeding the main one. When the glacier retreats it leaves a moraine, an unsorted ridge of till marking the former edge or snout of the ice, and meltwater flowing from it may build an outwash plain of layered gravel beyond the moraine. The sequence of erosion during advance and deposition during retreat is the key to reading the landscape.
questions.explanation: Marks require the identification plus one explanation per feature and a named landform of retreat, since recognising the agent alone is only the first step.
